grades.expert_take: Square-edge harshness with LSC maxed in means LSC is part of the problem: back LSC out to mid, then add HSC 1/4-1/2 turn for the jump-face bottoming; check rebound isn't packing and spring/sag suits ~200 lb geared at 6'4"; if still both, revalve.
grades.note: Right that more HSC can worsen square-edge harshness, but with LSC maxed it never says to back LSC to the 15-out standard and then add HSC for the face bottoming, which is the actual fix; ends on a spring/sag question.

grades.expert_take: 24 mm clamps (more offset than stock 22) means less trail and quicker steering, so they would make twitch and decel wobble worse; go the other way (less offset/steering damper), keep sag ~105, check rear spring isn't too stiff for 150 lb so rear isn't riding high, add a little fork comp to stop diving, check head bearing.
grades.note: Correctly notes more offset reduces trail and holds off on 24 mm clamps, with good dive-vs-packing split; doesn't plainly say 24 mm moves away from stability vs the 22 mm stock or mention a steering damper.
numbers_to_verify: 'Several testers found longer-offset clamps improved stability on this generation' (2022+ CRF250R stock offset is 22 mm; 24 mm reduces trail)

grades.expert_take: Too little sag with collar fully loose = spring too stiff or wrong free length, or bad measurement; re-measure (normal riding position, true fully-extended reading), check static sag and spring free length vs stock; if correct, go a step softer spring.
grades.note: Good catch that a 2025 350 SX-F has an air fork, correct 4.3 kg/mm = 42 N/mm, and the residual-preload/measurement checks are exactly right; doesn't say what to do if the checks pass (go a step softer).

grades.expert_take: 158 lb no gear is right in the stock window on a 2024 YZ250F; set race sag in Yamaha's range, check static, keep stock valving and tune clickers; revalve only for a specific complaint.
grades.note: Keeps stock springs and valving for a 158 lb C rider, catches the kg/mm vs N/mm mix-up, gives Yamaha's 90-100 mm sag and the free-sag test; what a pro would say.

grades.expert_take: With fork comp and shock HSC already at full soft, he's out of clicker range: needs a soft revalve for natural terrain; .44 springs fine for no jumps; check rebound, fork break-in/bushing friction.
grades.note: Correctly says he's out of clicker range and the money goes to a targeted revalve, not .44 springs, and asks the right dive-vs-stays-high question; no RM-Z specs cited.

grades.expert_take: Don't go much below ~130 psi or the fork rides low into its ramp and dives; harshness while not bottoming points to friction/valving/comp setting, not air; equalize/bleed, align, break-in; the stiffer rear spring also loads the front.
grades.note: Good: 155 psi stock, checks clicker direction, outer-chamber bleed, alignment, and a 3 psi test step; answers 'how low' only as 'not 102', no practical floor (~130).

grades.expert_take: For sand keep fork hold-up via air, not comp; fix braking-bump harshness with a touch less comp plus fork lower/lifted rear balance, and accel chop at shock with HSC out 1/4 and more sag toward 105; small steps.
grades.note: Sag 98->103-105 and keeping fork support for sand are the right calls, plus a faster-rebound test for packing; 'return to 13 out' is muddled since he's already at 13, accel chop at the shock HSC isn't addressed, and the 'five passes' coaching line is filler.

grades.expert_take: At ~213 geared start at the higher end (~165-170 psi), ride, then back off 2-3 psi at a time until it uses travel without bottoming; set shock spring/sag too.
grades.note: At 210-215 lb geared he asked which end to start; BAK picks the low end (155) and says weight doesn't justify more, where a tuner would start nearer the top (~165) for a heavy rider and back off; procedure is sound.
numbers_to_verify: 2018 KTM 250 SX-F AER48 manual pressure for a ~95-97 kg geared rider (likely ~10.8-11.0 bar / 157-160+ psi)

grades.expert_take: For trail: fork comp out 2-3 clicks, rebound out 1-2, forks ~flush/1-2 mm lower, shock LSC out 2-3, HSC out 1/4-1/2, sag ~105-108, rebound a touch faster; lower tire pressure.
grades.note: Safe ordered plan (fork comp 11->13 first, shock HSC/LSC only if needed) for a no-test race; a pro would give a fuller trail baseline (shock LSC/HSC out, a touch more sag) rather than one change.

grades.expert_take: Mostly technique (body back, stay on throttle off lip) for a returning rider; check stock settings are at standard, sag ~105, forks not set too soft/rebound too fast; ~200 geared is fine on stock springs.
grades.note: Balances technique and fork setup, gives stock 14/12 clickers and asks braking vs jump-face; doesn't give Kawasaki's sag target.

grades.expert_take: Check friction/break-in, bleed/equalize chambers, settings at standard, and the service history: overfilled oil in the damping/air side would cause stiffness; get oil volume checked to WP spec.
grades.note: Sensible: excess oil raises the deep-stroke ramp, low air makes it ride deep, bleed outer chambers, don't drain blind; no model so no spec, which is fair.

grades.expert_take: 375 lb is far beyond stock springs; give standard clicks but tell him he needs much stiffer springs both ends before clicker tuning means anything; safety on bottoming.
grades.note: Gives Honda standard clicks and correctly puts springs first; at 375 lb it should say flatly that stock and even the optional 5.0/52 springs are far too soft, rather than hedging.

grades.expert_take: 133 psi for 183 lb is at the low end; 2 in left for a slow rider is fine; harshness is comp/friction/valving, not pressure; try 135-140 and comp out; oil height change in AER is small effect.
grades.note: Gives a real-world ~140 psi number, explains why dropping air further can make it harsher, and says leave oil height alone; matches what a tuner would tell a 61-year-old 183 lb rider.
numbers_to_verify: Testers report ~10 psi pressure gain on hot days (seems high; typical a few psi)

grades.expert_take: Check engine mount/hanger and axle/pinch bolt torque, linkage bearings, tire pressure, fork oil/break-in; Honda chassis is stiff; harsh in pits points to tire/linkage/mounts, not valving.
grades.note: Right to rule out mounts, bearings, tire pressure and damper before chassis parts, and the 2025-26 CRF450R handlebar-clamp recall is real and relevant; no engine-hanger torque or tire-pressure numbers.

grades.expert_take: Stiffer rear spring raised the rear and loaded the front; at lower air the fork sits deep in its ramp, so go back UP in air (~140), comp back to mid, raise forks in clamps to rebalance, slow shock rebound for the stiffer spring.
grades.note: Correctly explains the stiffer rear loading the front and that dropping air made it ride deeper; return to 135/22 is sensible, but it doesn't suggest going up in air, raising the forks in the clamps or slowing shock rebound for the new spring.

grades.expert_take: 220 geared needs stiffer springs both ends on a 2019 YZ250F; one or two steps stiffer doesn't need a revalve, tune clickers; revalve optional later.
grades.note: Right answer (fork springs likely, check shock with free sag, no automatic revalve); refusing 2019 specs is over-cautious since the 2019 and 2020 YZ250F share the platform.

grades.expert_take: 5 ml of oil only changes end-stroke bottoming, not comfort; comfort is valving/comp; removing oil in-bike is impractical, drop the forks; stock springs probably OK at her weight, consider lowering for height.
grades.note: Answers the oil question directly (drop the forks), gives Honda's 380 ml, 5 ml steps and 5W, and correctly says 5 ml only changes end-stroke, not comfort; 'Start a guided job' is an in-app line.

grades.expert_take: Those settings are near full stiff comp front and rear with odd rebound; expect harsh, deflecting ride; reset all to standard; a previous owner likely heavier/faster or counted wrong direction.
grades.note: Clear table of found vs standard and what each change does, all directions correct; for a novice, resetting all four to standard rather than only fork compression would be the cleaner start.

grades.expert_take: Remove seat/side panels/muffler (subframe loosen if needed), use a punch and hammer or proper spanner; or pull the shock; check race sag to Kawasaki spec; 205 geared may need stiffer spring on X.
grades.note: Gives access (rear frame/airbox off), ring direction, stock 54 N/mm spring and preload range from the manual; long, lists tank and battery removal, and dismisses the common punch-and-hammer method.
numbers_to_verify: Whether the fuel tank and battery must come off to pull the KX250X rear frame for preload access

grades.expert_take: Use static sag to judge shock spring; little preload at 105 suggests spring OK or stiff; new cartridges need 3-5 hours break-in before judging; slap-downs need more shock comp/rebound, hands beat = fork comp/valving.
grades.note: Correct that slap-down harshness doesn't prove oversprung and free sag decides the shock spring, but gives no direction; a 1-hour-old conversion needs a few hours of break-in before judging, which it waves off.

grades.expert_take: ~230 lb needs stiffer fork and shock springs; valving can stay stock for a slow vet and tune clickers; revalve later if wanted.
grades.note: Correct plan for 230 lb (springs first, revalve optional), with Yamaha's 5.0/56 stock rates and sag; doesn't give a target spring range for his weight.

grades.expert_take: Start at the 2006 YZ125 manual standard clicks and sag; tune from there one change at a time.
grades.note: Labelled honestly as general, but the clicker table is a guess rather than the 2006 YZ125 manual baseline the rider asked for; sag guidance is fine.
numbers_to_verify: 2006 YZ125 manual standard clickers (fork comp/reb, shock LSC/HSC/reb) vs the 12/12/12/12/1.5 given

grades.expert_take: Fit a steering damper, check head-bearing tension, more sag/forks lower for stability, check shock rebound not kicking, more fork comp hold-up; it's partly rider position.
grades.note: Good mechanical checks and a useful accel-vs-braking question, but never mentions a steering damper, the standard fix for high-speed bar swapping, or sag/fork-height balance changes.

grades.expert_take: Learn to set sag (simple steps), set fork air to maker base for his weight, reset clickers to standard and change one at a time; likely needs stiffer shock spring; $1500 isn't first step.
grades.note: Exactly the pro answer: hold off on the $1,500, a clear step-by-step sag method, a full factory baseline, and change one thing at a time; fork pressure and 40-hour service figures aren't in the cited facts.
numbers_to_verify: 2020 Husqvarna FC 250 standard fork air pressure 10.4 bar (151 psi)
Husqvarna fork/shock service every 40 operating hours

grades.expert_take: Kicking: check sag/static (spring rate), try slower rebound in steps, check HSC; new 2023+ chassis; for the 125 SX start at standard; aftermarket shock is overkill first.
grades.note: Keeps the stock shock, gives KTM baselines and sag, checks chain and linkage, and the straight-up vs packing vs sideways split for rebound direction is what a tuner would say.

grades.expert_take: Lean it from stock for 5,700-8,000 ft: main down 2-3 sizes, pilot down one, needle clip up one, air screw out; use manual's altitude chart.
grades.note: Correct stock jetting from the manual and correct direction (leaner), but no concrete altitude starting change (main 2-3 smaller, clip up one, pilot down), which is what he asked; the % power estimate is filler.

grades.expert_take: MX bike lugged in tight woods fouls plugs: use maker premix ratio, hotter-correct plug, rev it/regear, clean power valve; ask for an enduro/EC map; don't swap sensors blind.
grades.note: Good: test the sensor rather than swap it, check fuel pressure/injector, notes the 15-hour piston service and the 1:60 spec; doesn't address that an MX bike lugged in tight woods on a 13T is itself a big contributor.

grades.expert_take: Rev it harder, use maker premix ratio, clean power valve, correct plug and idle, check air filter; TBI fouling usually use-related.
grades.note: Specs are cited, but brushing off low-rpm use and ruling out a hotter plug goes against the usual fix for a kid's 125 that never gets revved (the stock BR10 is very cold); diagnosis steps are fine.

grades.expert_take: Yes - Power Tuner values are offsets from stock, so a map of all zeros is the stock map.
grades.note: Yes, zero both grids since they're offsets, and upload to both slots; short and correct.

grades.expert_take: Snap-open dying at idle in neutral is common; add a few percent fuel in low throttle/low rpm cells, check idle; small steps.
grades.note: Sensible to check the filter seal and ask if it hesitates in gear, but he asked where and how much fuel; a pro would say snap-dying in neutral is common and suggest a small (+3-5%) enrichment in the low-throttle/low-rpm cells.
numbers_to_verify: Rideology app KX fuel/ignition grid size of 6 x 6 on the 2024 KX450

grades.expert_take: Best at 2-3 turns out means pilot too rich: drop one pilot size, re-set air screw ~1.5-2 out, check float height; 32:1 adds richness.
grades.note: Exactly right: air screw best at 2-3 out means the pilot is rich, go one size (#48) not two, check the 6.5 mm float height first.

grades.expert_take: Colder denser air needs richer: main up 1-2 sizes, needle clip down one (richer), maybe pilot up one.
grades.note: Correct: colder air needs richer, one main up, clip down one for the mid; doesn't mention pilot/air screw for the low end in the cold.

grades.expert_take: Idle hang-then-die after rebuild: air leak (boot, reeds, crank seals), pilot jet/float height, choke plunger seal; reconnect TPS.
grades.note: Good focus on pilot circuit, float level and air leaks, with a useful choke test, and tells him to restore TPS/timing; could push crank-seal/intake vacuum testing harder.

grades.expert_take: Intermittent cut-out: check kill switch/map switch wiring, harness chafing, grounds, battery, fuel pump connector/fuel filter; wiggle-test with engine running; warranty.
grades.note: Right priorities (connectors incl. TPS, tank vent, fuel delivery) and the 1-hour fuel-screen check from the manual is a good, specific catch; kill-switch wiring could be named.

grades.expert_take: TBI dies at idle: check intake air leaks, throttle body idle air / TPS calibration reset, dirty throttle body, battery voltage; warranty.
grades.note: Sensible order (idle adjuster function, TPS baseline, then intake/fuel), with the manual idle spec; generic but correct.

grades.expert_take: No O2 sensor, ECU won't add fuel for more air; gain is tiny; keep backfire screen in; new-bike plug fouling from idling.
grades.note: Correct: refit the screen, the ECU won't auto-compensate, and the 2021 CRF450R ECU update is a relevant check for fouling; could state plainly there's no O2 sensor so it can't add fuel.

grades.expert_take: Lean bog off idle: richen pilot/clip, check float height, air screw, power jet; give stock 2022 specs if known.
grades.note: Gives the stock 2022 YZ125 jetting he asked for and a sensible check-first plan; doesn't offer a first richening step for a lean off-idle bog.

grades.expert_take: Heat-related: check fuel tank vent, fuel pump/filter, connectors; restart resets; warranty.
grades.note: Heat-related fuel delivery/electrical with tank vent first is the right read and the restart-vs-cool question is useful; generic, no Honda-specific checks.

grades.expert_take: Most riders don't miss the switch; but confirm an older Vortex unit even plugs into the 2023+ harness; ask Vortex about updating.
grades.note: Gives a pick and correctly flags that older Vortex units may not suit the 2023+ bike at all, and that the switch also runs TC/launch/quickshift.

grades.expert_take: Plug-and-play on 2023+ models, app lets you choose/edit map settings within limits and GPS lap timing works; check model support.
grades.note: Generic; doesn't say what the KTM Connectivity Unit Offroad actually does (map/TC/launch settings via app, GPS lap timing) or which 2023+ models it plugs into; lots of 'not confirmed'.

grades.expert_take: Valve cover leak when hot after recall: re-check gasket/torque or reseal; check cooling system (coolant level, bleed, cap); gauge reading suspicious.
grades.note: Treats the ~350 reading as possible overheating, sends it back to recheck the recall repair, and the overfill check with Kawasaki capacities is useful; a bit cautious.

grades.expert_take: Check oil level for dealer overfill and air filter; blue smoke on new bike usually overfill; dealer fills oil in PDI.
grades.note: Answers the oil question, puts overfill/breather carryover first, and treats it as a warranty issue; right.

grades.expert_take: Stop riding; check engine mount bolts, wheels/sprocket, then drain oil/filter for metal; knock at idle suggests crank/rod, tear down.
grades.note: Stop, don't restart, check mounts and drain for metal, and lists crank/rod/balancer before the pump; what a race mechanic would say.

grades.expert_take: No fan on CRF250R; idling on stand boils it - don't; check coolant/bleed/cap; more oil won't help; fan kit if needed.
grades.note: Correct: more oil isn't the fix and idling on the stand boils a fanless bike; should say plainly the CRF250R has no fan, and is over-cautious on 2019 vs 2020 specs.

grades.expert_take: Most riders go longer than 15 h on a 300 SX; measure piston/cylinder at interval and decide; depends on riding.
grades.note: Correct that 15 h is KTM's piston replacement interval and that recreational riders often go longer based on inspection; no typical real-world range given.

grades.expert_take: Dealer PDI failure; brief run likely OK but document; compression/leak-down check; fast idle knob use when cold is normal on Honda; warranty.
grades.note: Right call: not break-in, stop cranking, dealer pressure test, fast-idle use when cold is normal, with Honda coolant specs.

grades.expert_take: 2023-24 CRF250R generally reliable; check valve clearances, service history, hours; known items small.
grades.note: Gives a pick and a sensible inspection list (clutch, filter sealing, valves); the 'upside-down filter clogs quickly' point is loose.

grades.expert_take: Recurring drip at weep hole after cover swap = shaft mechanical/oil seal; warranty again; minor seep can happen but recurring isn't normal.
grades.note: Correct: recurring weep-hole drips aren't normal, explains the weep hole, says identify coolant vs oil, and pushes warranty on the seal, not just the cover.

grades.expert_take: Hole under water pump is the weep hole; oil there means water pump oil seal leaking; correct oil level; warranty.
grades.note: Identifies the weep hole, oil there = pump oil seal, overfill doesn't explain it, warranty; with Kawasaki oil capacities.

grades.expert_take: Exhaust spigot spooge on new 2-stroke is normal-ish, harmless; check springs/O-rings, high-temp silicone; 40:1 is richer than KTM's 60:1.
grades.note: Correct: spooge at the pipe-to-cylinder joint (not head), 40:1 matches KTM's spec, harmless if small, check springs/seals and warranty if persistent.
